edges.description: Biofilm persistence and fungal biomass accumulation provoke host inflammatory response.
Inflammatory exudate combines with fungal biomass to obstruct the ear canal.

Ototopical drops suppress the commensal bacteria that normally compete with fungi for the canal surface, leaving the niche open. Recorded as triggering because the drug acts on the resident flora itself with nothing in between, even though the same exposure is only predisposing for the disease as a whole.

edges.description: Ambient heat and humidity keep the canal moist, working against the acidic, low-moisture state cerumen maintains. Graded lower than the antibiotic and trauma links in this entry because the evidence is a climate association asserted in a clinical series, with no measurement of cerumen pH, moisture, or peptide content.

Cleaning and instrumentation strip cerumen and abrade the epithelium beneath it, removing the barrier rather than merely weakening it. Recorded as triggering because the instrument acts on the barrier directly, with no intervening step.

edges.source: Systemic itraconazole for persistent Aspergillus otomycosis

nodes.description: Ototopical antibiotic use is the most common predisposing factor for otomycosis, found in approximately 47% of cases. Antibiotics suppress commensal bacteria that normally compete with fungi for nutrients and ecological niches, creating a permissive environment for fungal overgrowth. The resulting dysbiosis shifts the microbial community from bacterial-dominated to fungal-dominated.

nodes.description: Aspergillus-caused otomycosis carries a fixed species-level treatment gate: Aspergillus species are intrinsically resistant to fluconazole, so organism identification excludes that agent before isolate-level susceptibility results. This node is deliberately separate from the existing biofilm-resistance node and from acquired cyp51A or efflux-mediated azole resistance; neither of those isolate- or exposure-dependent mechanisms is sufficient for conformance to the module's intrinsic-resistance arm.

nodes.description: Colonizing fungi form biofilms on the ear canal epithelium. The biofilm extracellular matrix acts as a diffusion barrier that reduces antifungal drug penetration and mediates phenotypic drug resistance. This biofilm-mediated resistance contributes to treatment failure and recurrence rates of approximately 15%.

evidence.reference_title: Poly-(lactic-co-glycolic) Acid Nanoparticles Entrapping Pterostilbene for Targeting Aspergillus Section Nigri.
evidence.snippet: the PLGA-NPs system can increase the bioavailability of PTB in Aspergillus section Nigri biofilm by overcoming the biofilm matrix barrier and delivering PTB to fungal cells.

evidence.reference_title: Relapsing Aspergillus otomycosis despite prolonged systemic antifungal therapy and resolution after topical voriconazole administration: A case report.
evidence.snippet: otomycosis relapsed even after six months of continuous systemic antifungal treatment with therapeutic drug levels and without treatment interruption; and only resolved after application of topical voriconazole

nodes.description: The combination of fungal biomass (hyphae, spores, conidiophores), inflammatory exudate, and desquamated epithelium accumulates in the external auditory canal, producing the characteristic clinical symptoms of pruritus, otalgia, discharge, and conductive hearing impairment. The degree of obstruction correlates with the severity of hearing loss.

evidence.reference_title: Clinicopathological study of otomycosis in a tertiary hospital in South-west Nigeria.
evidence.snippet: common presenting complaint was itchy ear (33.8%). Majority of patients (85.9%) had unilateral ear involvement

nodes.description: The external auditory canal is normally protected by cerumen, which maintains an acidic pH (mean ~3.95), contains antimicrobial peptides (defensins hBD1-3, cathelicidin LL-37, lysozyme, lactoferrin, BPI), and supports colonization resistance by resident microbiota. Physical or chemical disruption of this barrier by excessive ear cleaning, moisture exposure, or other trauma removes the primary antimicrobial defense.

cell_types: Epithelial cell of external acoustic meatus

evidence.reference_title: Human antimicrobial proteins in ear wax.
evidence.snippet: All ten antimicrobial peptides are present in ear wax. Some of these proteins seem to be merelycell-bound in ear wax. Antimicrobial peptides in ear wax prevent bacteria and fungi from causing infections inthe external auditory canal.

evidence.reference_title: The Importance of Ear Canal Microbiota and Earwax in the Prevention of Outer Ear Infections.
evidence.snippet: Earwax is composed primarily of keratin secreted by epithelial cells and substances secreted by sweat and apocrine glands. It plays a key role in the physiology of the ear canal, maintaining a low pH, limiting moisture, and exhibiting antimicrobial properties.

nodes.description: Compulsive ear cleaning and instrumentation damage the epithelial lining and remove protective cerumen, predisposing to fungal colonization.

nodes.description: Aspergillus and Candida species colonize the external auditory canal when the microenvironment becomes permissive. Aspergillus species (particularly A. niger and A. flavus) are the most commonly isolated pathogens, followed by Candida species (particularly C. parapsilosis and C. tropicalis). The species distribution varies by geographic region.

nodes.description: Fungal hyphae, spores, and biofilm debris provoke local innate immune activation in the external auditory canal. Neutrophils and other innate immune cells are recruited to the site, producing inflammatory mediators that cause tissue edema, erythema, and pain. The host defense response to fungus is activated but insufficient to clear the biofilm-protected infection.

nodes.description: The Aspergillus and Candida agents that cause otomycosis retain fungal sterol 14-alpha-demethylase activity in their ergosterol pathways. This normal Cyp51/Erg11 activity is the disease-local therapeutic vulnerability inhibited by viable imidazole and triazole agents. Its presence does not imply that every azole inhibits every organism: the Aspergillus fluconazole-specific intrinsic resistance gate and isolate-level susceptibility remain separate constraints.

evidence.reference_title: Sterol 14α-Demethylase Ligand-Binding Pocket-Mediated Acquired and Intrinsic Azole Resistance in Fungal Pathogens.
evidence.snippet: The fungal cytochrome P450 enzyme sterol 14α-demethylase (SDM) is a key enzyme in the ergosterol biosynthesis pathway.

nodes.description: Persistent Aspergillus otomycosis requiring systemic treatment can use itraconazole, a triazole that inhibits fungal Cyp51/Erg11. Itraconazole does not reverse the lineage-level fluconazole exclusion, and isolate susceptibility can still impose additional restrictions.

nodes.description: Topical clotrimazole is a commonly used imidazole treatment for otomycosis. It inhibits fungal Cyp51/Erg11 while bypassing the fluconazole-specific intrinsic exclusion in Aspergillus. This does not imply universal clotrimazole susceptibility; isolate-level resistance can impose additional restrictions.

evidence.snippet: In the 12th week after treatment, 76.34% of the 10% povidone-iodine group and 85.26% of the Clotrimazole group had a good response to treatment (p = 0.248).

nodes.description: Topical miconazole is an imidazole alternative to clotrimazole for otomycosis, inhibiting the same fungal Cyp51/Erg11 sterol-demethylase target. Miconazole oil formulations are the subject of two Phase III trials in otomycosis.

evidence.snippet: The intention of the study is to evaluate the efficacy of Miconazole Oil on fungal infection of the ears when applied using 5 drops into the ear(s) twice daily for 14 days continuously.
